# Design: lighter SMP lock, interrupt, time and tick paths

Status: **implemented and measured in emulation**. Six changes remove barriers, supervisor calls, locks, SGIs and interrupts that protect no shared state, in the FreeRTOS SMP port, the SMP newlib runtime, the platform counter clock and the cached eight-core platform. Each follows the reference implementation named in its section. The newlib lookup and the counter clock are on `work/mc-perf-a-1025` and can merge on their own. The lock bookkeeping, IRQ exit, wake placement and late-tick changes build on that branch and merge only after a board session passes. The first session, on port 3-3 on 2026-10-25, ran cleanly but failed its cycle criterion because its measurement timed lock contention (below); they stay off `bringup` until the revised measurement of [the multicore performance runbook](../board-runbooks/multicore-performance-session.md) passes. Fair spinlocks, cache-line relayout, a different `-march` and an IRQ entry without the floating-point save also need a supervised board session and are not part of this design.

The port sources are the patches `patches/freertos-smp-c.patch`, `patches/freertos-smp-asm.patch` and `patches/freertos-smp-tasks.patch`, which `cmake/a733-smp-cached.cmake` applies to the pinned FreeRTOS-Kernel `97f50c0e`; `cmake/smp.cmake` applies the first two for the QEMU targets. Line numbers below refer to the patched files.

## Measurement

Three tools measure the base tree and each change:

- [checks/smp-port-cost.py](../../checks/smp-port-cost.py) builds a two-core
  QEMU image and counts `INST_RETIRED` under `-icount shift=0`, where the count
  is exact, on `cortex-a55` and `cortex-a76` cores. Each figure is the least
  of 16 samples minus an empty region, or a mean over 256 round trips or 64
  wakes. The check now also counts:
  - an SGI that an EL1 task sends to its own core, from the send to the
    task's next instruction;
  - one uncontended counter clock read;
  - an unpinned task that each tick wakes while both cores are idle, also in
    an image whose two cores have different types;
  - `__getreent`, in a second image built with the SMP newlib runtime.
- [checks/a733-smp-cached.py](../../checks/a733-smp-cached.py) `--count` runs
  the cached eight-core diagnostic in the instruction model and gives the
  median instructions, `SVC`, `DSB`, `DMB` and `ISB` per call and per IRQ,
  from vector entry to exception return. `--late-ticks 5` puts the counter
  five periods past the pending tick deadline while core 0 has no IRQ in
  progress. The model now treats the timer PPI as level-sensitive, as the GIC
  does, and reports `CNTP_CTL_EL0.ISTATUS`; it used to deliver a tick IRQ again
  after its EOI when the handler spanned a scheduling quantum.
- [checks/clock-counter-contention.c](../../checks/clock-counter-contention.c)
  runs the counter clock on 16 host threads, 200,000 calls each, with
  modeled counter reads.

QEMU on an x86-64 host and the instruction model execute the real instructions, but neither reproduces the Arm memory model. QEMU runs on a host whose stores are seen in order, and the model interleaves the cores one quantum at a time over shared host memory. Neither can show a missing or misplaced barrier, so the ordering argument for the counter clock below rests on reasoning until a board session tests it. The same holds for the lock bookkeeping and the IRQ exit barriers: the emulators show which instructions go, and only the board session can show that the remaining barriers order what the reasoning below says they order.

## Lock bookkeeping without `DSB`

`vPortRecursiveLock` reads and writes two kinds of bookkeeping word through `prvGet64` and `prvSet64` (`port.c` 1696–1715): a lock's recursion count, which only the lock's holder accesses, and a core's ownership bits, which only that core accesses. Each wrapped its access in `DSB SY`, which made a critical-section pair execute 24 `DSB SY`. The wrappers are now plain `volatile` accesses, and 22 of the 24 go.

A core observes its own accesses in program order, so neither word needs a barrier on its own core. Between holders, the releasing core writes the recursion count before the `DMB SY` and the gate store in `prvSpinUnlock`, and the next holder reads it after the `DMB SY` that follows a successful `prvSpinTrylock`. A Linux arm64 spinlock orders its holders' data the same way, with the acquiring compare-and-swap of `queued_spin_lock` and the release store of `queued_spin_unlock` (Linux v6.17 `include/asm-generic/qspinlock.h` 107–129). The message-passing tests of the Arm Architecture Reference Manual (DDI 0487, appendix K11, which this project has not cached) require no more. The two `DSB SY` that remain are in `prvSpinUnlock`, one per lock release, before the `SEV` that wakes a waiter in `WFE`.

## newlib state from the task register

`__getreent` (`runtime/newlib_smp.c`) took supervisor call 118, which masks IRQs and indexes `pxCurrentTCBs` by core. Once a core has resumed a task, bits [47:0] of `TPIDRRO_EL0` already hold that task's control block, which EL0 can read, and `xTaskGetCurrentTaskHandle` reads it with one `MRS` ([docs/smp.md](../smp.md#port-operations-avoid-supervisor-calls-and-shared-lines)). `__getreent` now returns the reentrancy structure inside that block. A task's own block does not change when it migrates, so the read needs no mask; ESP-IDF v5.3.1 returns the current task's block without a lock for the same reason (`components/freertos/esp_additions/freertos_tasks_c_additions.h` 849–867). The structure's offset comes from `StaticTask_t`, and `platform/qemu-smp/freertos_tasks_c_additions.h` asserts that it equals the control block's. While the register's task field is zero, before the core has resumed a task, `__getreent` keeps supervisor call 118, which returns the global state before the scheduler starts.

## Counter clock without a lock

`a733_counter_clock_now` (`platform/a733/counter_clock.c`) serialized every caller behind a ticket lock with interrupts masked and faulted the provider when a sample fell below the last one. Two cores read `CNTPCT_EL0` at slightly different times, so a sample taken after another core's can still be a tick lower; serialized behind that core, it faulted the provider. A caller stalled while holding its ticket also faulted every waiter after 100 microseconds.

Each call now reads the counter after `ISB`, as Linux `__arch_counter_get_cntpct` does (`arch/arm64/include/asm/arch_timer.h` 179–189), with no lock and no mask. The shared history only rises: a caller raises it to its own sample with a compare-and-swap, or reports the history when its sample is not above it. A failed swap reloads the history and samples again, so a stalled caller cannot lower the history or delay another caller. Each sample is taken after the history it is compared with was loaded, so a lower sample shows skew between cores. The history word keeps its own cache line, apart from the fault flag that every caller reads.

The provider now absorbs any backward step of up to 100 microseconds, whatever its cause, and reports the history instead; only a larger step faults it. A real counter regression smaller than that is no longer detected. The bound must stay far above the measured skew between the A55 and A76 cores' counter reads, which no board session has measured yet.

The history uses relaxed atomics. Every caller's result lies between the history it loaded and the history after its swap, and coherence orders all accesses to that one word, so a call that happens after another returns no earlier time. That argument covers a single location only and needs no barrier; the board session must still confirm it on the A55 and A76 cores. The contention check adds the skew, stalled-caller and skew-bound cases; the base provider faults in the first two.

## IRQ exit barriers

The IRQ exit (`portASM.S`, `FreeRTOS_IRQ_Handler`) executed `DSB SY` and `ISB` after `MSR DAIFSET`, and `DSB SY` and `ISB` after writing `SPSR_EL1` and `ELR_EL1` on both of its exits. Three barriers go:

- The `ISB` after `MSR DAIFSET, #2`. A `DAIFSet` write masks IRQs from the
  next instruction: Linux `kernel_exit` masks with `disable_daif`
  (`arch/arm64/kernel/entry.S` 335–337; `arch/arm64/include/asm/assembler.h`
  37–39) and `local_irq_disable` with `msr daifset, #3`
  (`arch/arm64/include/asm/irqflags.h` 52–57), both without `ISB`. The mask
  is needed because the FromISR critical section of the tick handler ends with
  `MSR DAIFCLR`.
- The `DSB SY` and `ISB` before `ERET` on the exit that returns to the
  interrupted task. `ERET` uses the `SPSR_EL1` and `ELR_EL1` just written and
  is a context synchronization event, which also completes the EOI. Linux
  `kernel_exit` writes `ELR_EL1` and `SPSR_EL1` and returns with no barrier
  between (`entry.S` 412–461); its `dmb sy` before `eret` is the Cortex-A77
  erratum 1508412 workaround, which neither A733 core needs. TF-A `el3_exit`
  does the same at EL3 (`lib/el3_runtime/aarch64/context.S` 656–681, TF-A
  `0892ad4d`).
- The `DSB SY` and `ISB` on the exit that switches context. `portSAVE_CONTEXT`
  reads `SPSR_EL1` and `ELR_EL1` back with `MRS`, which observes the writes in
  program order, and another core that resumes the saved task is ordered by
  the kernel locks that `vTaskSwitchContext` takes. `portRESTORE_CONTEXT`
  keeps its own `DSB SY` and `ISB` after the PMR write.

One `DSB SY` stays before `MSR ICC_EOIR1_EL1`, so a handler's device write that clears a level interrupt completes before the EOI. Linux's `gic_eoi_irq` has no such `DSB` (`drivers/irqchip/irq-gic-v3.c` 719–722); it stays because no reference shows it unneeded with these device drivers. Linux follows the EOI write with `isb()` (line 722) because the kernel keeps running after it and must see the priority drop before it unmasks. This exit needs no `ISB` there: the next instruction that depends on the EOI is the `ERET`, which is itself a context synchronization event, and on the switching exit the `ISB` after the PMR write in `portRESTORE_CONTEXT` precedes it too.

The SGI handler's per-core count (`platform/a733-smp-cached/platform.c`) was an atomic add. Only its own core writes it, so it is now a relaxed load and store, which other cores' relaxed loads still read untorn.

## Wake placement

`prvYieldForTask` (`tasks.c` 933–945) chooses the core running the lowest priority below the woken task's. Its `<=` comparison gave a tie to the last such core, so when several cores were idle the task went to the highest-numbered idle core and cost an SGI. An idle calling core, once chosen, now keeps a tie against another idle core of its own type: its yield needs no SGI, and the task runs where its waker's data is cached. An idle core of another type still takes the tie, so an idle Cortex-A76 still wins over an idle Cortex-A55. Ties between busy cores, and ties that the calling core does not hold, still go to the last such core. Linux `select_idle_sibling` returns the target CPU when it is idle and `asym_fits_cpu` accepts its capacity (`kernel/sched/fair.c` 7751–7753).

`configCORES_SHARE_TYPE(a, b)` names the cores of one type and defaults to all cores alike. The cached A733 configuration (`platform/a733-smp-cached/FreeRTOSConfig.h`) defines it from `A733_SMP_A55_MASK` in `include/a733_smp_placement.h`, which every cached image now includes; the cached and storage build identities hash that header. In QEMU every one of 64 tick wakes of an unpinned task now runs on the tick's core, and both cores retire 7% fewer instructions per wake. In an image whose configuration gives the two QEMU cores different types, none does.

On the A733, a task that may run on every core and is woken by the tick on core 0 still goes to idle core 7, as before. The rule changes placement for tasks confined to one cluster, such as the integrated OS image's tasks without an explicit placement, which stay on the A55 cores.

## Late ticks in up to three calls per IRQ

The cached platform's tick acknowledgement advances the compare value by one period. A tick IRQ taken N periods late therefore left the compare value in the past, and the timer fired N more times in a row. The tick IRQ (`platform/a733-smp-cached/platform.c`) now works as follows:

- It reads `CNTP_CTL_EL0.ISTATUS` and processes no tick when the timer
  condition no longer holds, as Linux's timer handler acts only on `ISTATUS`
  (`drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c` 671).
- After the first tick handler call it reads `ISTATUS` again. When the
  condition still holds, the IRQ was late and at least one more period is
  due. It makes at most three tick handler calls in all, as
  `hrtimer_interrupt` retries at most three times (`hrtimer.c` 1921–1922),
  so one comparison of the counter with the next deadline plus a period
  decides whether a third call is due, where `hrtimer_forward` divides
  (`kernel/time/hrtimer.c` 1042–1074). The level-sensitive timer interrupt
  is taken again for any period still due.
- Each call advances the compare value by one period, so the next deadline
  stays in phase. Linux programs its next event from the current count
  instead (`arm_arch_timer.c` 741–757); keeping the phase keeps the kernel's
  tick count equal to the elapsed periods.
- A counter read taken early can only lower the count of due periods. The
  first call relies on the IRQ mask of exception entry; the further calls
  mask IRQs again, because the tick handler's FromISR critical section
  clears `PSTATE.I`.
